13830:
To revitalize something means to bring it back to a state of energy, strength, and active life after it has become weak, tired, slow, or dull. Think of it as pressing a "bring back to life" button — not making something entirely new, but restoring the lively, strong quality it once had.

A simple way to feel the word: imagine a plant that has wilted from neglect. You water it, give it sunlight, and slowly it stands tall again, full of life. That process — that act of making something thrive again after decline — is essentially what revitalize means.
The Most Important Idea Inside This Word

The single most important thing to understand about "revitalize" is that it almost always implies three things happening together:

Something was once good, energetic, or strong → it declined, weakened, or lost its energy → now someone or something is making it good again.

This means revitalize is not about creating energy from scratch. It is about recovering energy or life that was lost. This is what separates it from words like "energize" or "activate." When you revitalize, there is always a sense of bringing back something that slipped away.

Almost anything that can have "life" or "energy" — literally or figuratively — can be revitalized. Here are the major categories you will encounter in real life:

People and the body. A long vacation can revitalize a burnt-out worker. A good meal can revitalize someone who hasn't eaten all day. Here, revitalize means restoring physical or mental energy to a person who had run low on it.

Places and communities. A city government might revitalize a neglected neighborhood by building parks, cleaning streets, and attracting new businesses. Here, it means making a place active, thriving, and livable again after it had become rundown or forgotten.

Organizations, brands, and economies. A new CEO might revitalize a struggling company. A government might revitalize a country's economy after a recession. Here, revitalize means restoring productivity, growth, and momentum to a system that had stalled.

Relationships and emotions. A couple might take a trip together to revitalize their relationship. Here, revitalize means restoring warmth, connection, and excitement that had quietly faded over time.

Cultures, traditions, and ideas. A movement might revitalize an ancient art form or a tradition that was dying out. Here, it means breathing new life into something the world was slowly forgetting.

"Revitalize" suggests a significant, meaningful transformation — not just a small boost. It implies that the decline was real and noticeable, and that the recovery is also real and substantial. It is a powerful, deliberate word.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "This coffee refreshed me." → A small, pleasant lift.
  • "This coffee revitalized me." → I was genuinely exhausted, and now I feel meaningfully restored.

The second sentence carries far more weight. Use "revitalize" when the change matters.
The Tone and Feeling of This Word

Revitalize is an inherently positive and hopeful word. It carries a sense of renewal and optimism. When something is revitalized, the feeling is that things are genuinely getting better. Because of this, the word is especially common in speeches, plans, proposals, and motivational writing — anywhere people want to inspire confidence that recovery or transformation is possible.
How It Works in a Sentence

Revitalize is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — something or someone being revitalized. You can never just say "they revitalized" and stop there. You revitalize something.

Here are examples showing how it appears in different structures:

Active voice (someone is doing the revitalizing):

  • "The new coach revitalized the entire team."
  • "A single bold decision revitalized the company."

Passive voice (the focus is on what was revitalized):

  • "The neighborhood was revitalized after years of neglect."
  • "Her confidence was revitalized by the kind feedback."

Ongoing action:

  • "The city is working to revitalize its downtown area."

Even nature can revitalize:

  • "The long rain revitalized the dry, cracked earth."
How Revitalize Differs From Similar Words

These words are close in meaning, but each has its own shade. Understanding the differences will sharpen your feel for "revitalize" significantly.

Revive is very similar, but it is often more urgent and immediate. You revive someone who has fainted — it's about bringing something back from a near-complete stop. Revitalize implies a more gradual, sustained effort over time, not just a sudden jolt.

Rejuvenate focuses more on making something feel younger or fresher. It has a stronger connection to youthfulness and freshness. You might rejuvenate your skin with a good cream, but you would revitalize a city's economy.

Restore means to return something to its exact original condition — like restoring an old painting to look precisely as it once did. Revitalize doesn't demand going back to the original. It simply means making something energetic and thriving again, even if that looks somewhat different from before.

Refresh is much lighter. Refreshing gives a minor, pleasant boost. Revitalizing is a deeper, more substantial renewal that implies real previous decline.

Reinvigorate is the closest synonym to revitalize. The subtle difference is that reinvigorate emphasizes restoring vigor and strength specifically, while revitalize is broader — it includes restoring life, energy, purpose, and activity in a fuller sense.
The Most Common Phrases You Will Encounter

In real reading and conversation, you will most often hear "revitalize" paired with words like these: revitalize the economy, revitalize a neighborhood, revitalize a brand, revitalize a relationship, revitalize downtown, revitalize one's passion, revitalize a career.

Noticing these common pairings will help you use the word naturally and recognize it instantly in context.

To revitalize something means to bring it back to a condition of energy, strength, and active life after it had lost those qualities — making it genuinely thrive again in a way that is meaningful and lasting.
13831:
A revival is what happens when something that had faded away, stopped, or nearly died comes back to life again.

Think of it this way: something existed, then it weakened or disappeared, and then — it returned. That return is the revival.

The word always carries this three-part idea:

  1. Something existed before.
  2. It declined, stopped, or was forgotten.
  3. It came back.

Without that sense of "something was lost and now it's back," the word doesn't quite fit. That's what makes revival different from just "a beginning" — it's specifically a return.

Almost anything that can decline can also have a revival. Here are the major areas:

1. Interest or Popularity

When something that was once popular goes out of fashion and then becomes popular again, we call it a revival.

Vinyl records had a huge revival in the 2010s — people started buying them again after decades of near-disappearance.

There's been a revival of interest in home cooking since the pandemic.

This is the most general and everyday use of the word.

2. Something That Was Stopped or Inactive

A project, a tradition, a practice, or even a relationship that stopped and then restarted can be called a revival.

The revival of the peace talks gave people hope.

The festival had been cancelled for years, but its revival last summer drew thousands of visitors.

3. A Religious Revival

In a religious context, revival has a specific and important meaning: a period when large numbers of people in a community suddenly become deeply interested in religion again, often after a time of spiritual coldness or low participation.

This kind of revival usually involves intense emotion, public prayer, conversions, and a sense of spiritual renewal sweeping through a community or even an entire region.

The Great Awakening was a powerful religious revival in 18th-century America that changed how people practiced their faith.

The word revival is also used to refer to the actual event or gathering that tries to spark this religious renewal — a "revival meeting" or just "a revival" — where a preacher leads services over several days or weeks to reawaken people's faith.

She attended a revival at the church every summer growing up.

4. A Theatre or Performance Revival

When an old play, musical, or opera is brought back and produced again on stage — often with a fresh cast and updated staging — that production is called a revival.

The revival of West Side Story on Broadway received standing ovations every night.

It was a revival, not a remake — the original script was kept intact.

This use is very common in theatre and arts journalism.

5. Economic Revival

When an economy, a business, or an industry that was struggling or in decline begins to grow and thrive again, that's an economic revival.

The region saw an economic revival after the new factories opened.

The brand's revival under new management surprised the entire industry.

6. A Person's Revival (Health or Consciousness)

Though less common, the word can describe when a person who was unconscious, weak, or near death recovers or is brought back to consciousness.

The doctor's quick action led to the patient's revival.

This use overlaps with the verb "revive," which means to restore someone to consciousness or health.

Revival is generally a positive word. It suggests hope, renewal, and a second chance. When we say something is experiencing a revival, there's usually a sense of excitement — something good that was lost has been found again.

However, revival can be neutral or even cautionary depending on context:

There are fears of a revival of old hostilities between the two nations.

Here, the revival of something bad — conflict — is clearly not being celebrated. So the word itself is neutral in that it simply describes the return of something; whether that's good or bad depends on what is returning.
How Revival Differs From Similar Words

These words are related but each has a slightly different shade of meaning:

Renewal — focuses on freshness and making something new again. A renewal feels forward-looking and clean. A revival, by contrast, feels like a return to something specific from the past.

A renewal of your passport = you're continuing it.
A revival of an old tradition = you're bringing back something that stopped.

Recovery — often used for health or economics and implies returning to a normal or stable state after damage. Recovery is about reaching a floor; revival often implies something more energetic and visible — a return to strength or prominence, not just stability.

Restoration — means returning something to its original condition, usually physical (restoring a painting, a building). Revival is about returning life, energy, or activity — not necessarily a physical original state.

Resurgence — close to revival, but resurgence often implies something coming back suddenly and powerfully, sometimes in an unwanted way (a resurgence of a disease). Revival has a broader, more positive range.

Knowing which words commonly appear next to "revival" helps you use it naturally:

  • A revival of interest in something
  • Economic/cultural/religious revival
  • Stage a revival (to cause or bring about a revival)
  • A revival meeting (a religious gathering)
  • Experience a revival
  • Lead a revival
  • A Broadway revival (a new production of an old show)
  • A revival of old tensions/hostilities (negative use)

Revival is a noun that names the return of something that had faded, stopped, or declined. The thing could be interest, a tradition, a religion, a performance, an economy, or a person's consciousness — the word works across all these areas.

The key insight to hold onto: revival requires something to have been lost first. No loss, no revival. That sense of "something came back from near-death or long sleep" is what gives the word its particular power and warmth.
13832:
To revive means to bring something back to life, strength, activity, or awareness after it had weakened, stopped, or nearly disappeared.

The key idea locked inside this word is a three-stage story:

  1. Something was once alive, active, or strong.
  2. It weakened, faded, went still, or nearly died.
  3. Now it comes back — it is restored to life or vigor.

That movement — from decline back to vitality — is exactly what "revive" captures. Without that sense of "it was there before, then it faded, now it's back," the word doesn't quite fit.

Revive works in two grammatical modes:

1. Transitive — you revive something or someone (you are the cause)

"The doctors revived the patient."
"They revived the old tradition."

Here, an outside force acts on something and brings it back.

2. Intransitive — something revives on its own

"She slowly revived after the shock."
"Interest in the band revived years later."

Here, no external actor is named — the subject itself comes back.
The Many Situations Where "Revive" Is Used

This word is flexible. It travels across many different areas of life. Here are the main ones:

1. Reviving a Person (Medical or Physical)

When someone has fainted, is unconscious, or is in a life-threatening state, to revive them means to restore their consciousness or functioning. This is the most literal use of the word.

"The paramedics used CPR to revive the man who collapsed on the street."
"She splashed cold water on her face to revive herself after feeling dizzy."
"Smelling salts were used to revive the boxer who was knocked out."

The person was not fully conscious or functional — and then they were brought back.

2. Reviving a Plant or Living Thing

A wilted, dried-out, or seemingly dying plant can be revived with water, sunlight, or care. The plant hasn't quite died — but it has come very close, and something brings it back.

"He revived the dying plant by watering it regularly."
"After the drought ended, the garden slowly revived."

3. Reviving a Feeling, Emotion, or Mood

Feelings like hope, love, enthusiasm, fear, or sadness can "die down" inside a person. When something brings that feeling back to the surface with strength, it revives it.

"Seeing her childhood home revived a flood of old memories."
"The speech revived the crowd's enthusiasm."
"His kind words revived her hope when she had nearly given up."

4. Reviving a Tradition, Custom, or Practice

When a cultural tradition, a ritual, an art form, or a custom falls out of use over time, someone can deliberately bring it back — reviving it.

"The festival was revived after a gap of fifty years."
"Several local musicians are trying to revive folk music in the region."
"The school revived the annual science fair that had been discontinued."

5. Reviving an Economy, Business, or Industry

When a business, economy, or sector has been performing poorly — struggling, shrinking, or nearly collapsing — efforts to restore its health are described as reviving it.

"The new policies were designed to revive the struggling economy."
"The company brought in new leadership to revive its declining sales."
"Tourism helped revive the coastal town after years of hardship."

6. Reviving a Play, Film, Show, or Creative Work

In the world of entertainment and arts, an old show, play, or series that is brought back for a new audience or a new run is said to be revived.

"The classic Broadway musical was revived with an entirely new cast."
"The director revived the 1980s action franchise for modern audiences."
"The streaming platform revived the cancelled sitcom after fan demand."

7. Reviving a Conversation, Debate, or Idea

Discussions, arguments, or ideas that had faded away from people's attention can be revived — brought back into focus.

"The new evidence revived the debate about the city's history."
"His article revived interest in a theory that had been largely forgotten."
"An old rivalry between the two teams was revived after years of peace."

"Revive" always implies that something existed and flourished before. You cannot revive something that was never alive or active in the first place. This separates "revive" from words like create, start, or build.

Compare:

  • "They created a new tradition." (It didn't exist before — it's new.)
  • "They revived an old tradition." (It existed before, faded, and is now back.)

Also, to revive something doesn't always mean it was completely dead — it may have only weakened or faded. Think of it on a spectrum: reviving can mean pulling something back from complete death, or simply from being dull, tired, or inactive.

Restore — to bring something back to its original condition. Restoration is often about returning to an exact previous state (restoring a painting, restoring power). Revive is broader and more about bringing life and energy back, not necessarily an exact original form.

Resuscitate — almost always used in a strict medical context (restoring breathing and heartbeat). Revive is broader and can be used metaphorically in many areas.

Renew — to make something fresh again or extend it (renewing a subscription, renewing energy). Renew often involves refreshing or starting a new cycle. Revive carries a stronger sense of rescue from decline or return from near-death.

Rekindle — specifically used for bringing back fire, passion, love, or emotional warmth. It's narrower. Revive can cover all those things and much more.

"A strong cup of tea revived her after the long journey."
"Nothing could revive his interest in the project once he had lost faith in it."
"The rain revived the dry, cracked earth."
"She tried to revive the dying conversation with a funny story."
"Doctors worked for twenty minutes before they finally revived him."
"His old mentor's advice revived something in him that had been dormant for years."

"Revive" carries a quietly hopeful tone. When you say something is being revived, there is an implied sense of rescue, recovery, or renewal. It suggests that something worth preserving has not been fully lost — and that is good news. The word feels like a second chance.
13833: To revivify something means to bring it back to life, energy, or vitality after it had grown weak, dull, lifeless, or inactive. Think of it as breathing fresh life and vigor into something that had lost its spark. When you revivify something, you're not just waking it up — you're restoring it to a state of being fully alive and vibrant again.

Revivify is a word with real force to it. It doesn't just mean "to fix" or "to improve" something. It carries the specific sense of restoring the life force of something — its spirit, energy, and vitality. The key idea is that whatever is being revivified had once been alive and thriving, then faded or stagnated, and is now being brought back to that original state of energy and life.
How it differs from similar words

Revivify is close in meaning to several other words, but each has its own shade of meaning:

Revive is the most common and closest word. You revive someone who fainted, or you revive a trend. Revivify is more formal and more emphatic — it stresses the restoration of deep, full vitality, not just basic existence. If revive is turning the lights back on, revivify is flooding the room with brilliant light.

Reinvigorate means to give new strength and energy to something. It's very close to revivify, but reinvigorate focuses more on strength and drive, while revivify focuses more on life and spirit.

Rejuvenate means to make something feel young and fresh again. It often implies making something seem newer or more youthful. Revivify doesn't carry that "youthfulness" angle — it's about restoring vitality, regardless of age.

Resurrect means to bring something back from the dead, often literally or dramatically. Revivify is softer — it doesn't require something to be fully dead, just depleted or dormant.

Revivify is a formal and literary word. You'll encounter it in serious writing — academic papers, literary fiction, high-quality journalism, formal speeches, and essays. It's not a word you'd use in casual everyday conversation ("Hey, let's revivify this party!" would sound strange). In conversation, people would more naturally say revive, breathe new life into, or reinvigorate.

It's most commonly used to talk about abstract things rather than living creatures. You revivify ideas, movements, traditions, art forms, relationships, organizations, economies, cultures, and so on. For example, a new leader might revivify a struggling political party. A filmmaker might revivify a dying genre. A breakthrough discovery might revivify a field of science that had gone stale.

You can also use it to describe revivifying a person's spirit or morale — not their physical body, but their inner energy and enthusiasm. For example, a wonderful vacation might revivify a person who has been burned out and exhausted for months.

Here are several examples, moving from simpler to more complex, so you can see how naturally the word fits into different contexts:

"The new coach completely revivified the team, who had lost all confidence after years of defeat."

"Her passionate speech revivified the movement, drawing thousands of new supporters who had grown apathetic."

"The young artist's bold new style revivified a genre of painting that critics had written off as dead."

"Spending a month in the countryside revivified him — he returned to the city feeling like a completely new person."

"The government's investment in the region revivified a local economy that had been stagnant for over a decade."
All the tense forms you need

Since you want to be fully equipped with this word:

  • Base form: revivify
  • Third person singular (present): revivifies → "She revivifies everything she touches."
  • Past tense: revivified → "The funding revivified the project."
  • Present participle: revivifying → "The new policy is revivifying the town's economy."
  • Past participle: revivified → "The tradition, once revivified, spread quickly."
A simple way to remember it

Picture something you love — a garden, a friendship, a community — that has gone grey, quiet, and lifeless over time. Now picture someone pouring pure energy and life back into it until it blooms and thrives again. That action — that deliberate, powerful restoration of life and vitality — is exactly what it means to revivify something.
13834:
Revocation is the official act of taking back, canceling, or withdrawing something that was previously granted, issued, or put into force. When something is revoked, it is no longer valid. The authority or person who originally gave or created something uses their power to undo it — to make it cease to exist going forward.

A simple way to picture it: imagine a museum gives you a membership card that lets you enter for free. Later, for some reason, the museum decides to cancel your membership and takes the card back. That act of officially canceling what was once given to you is revocation. Now apply that same logic to licenses, legal rights, contracts, wills, and permissions — that is the territory where the word "revocation" truly belongs.

Three things are always present when a true revocation occurs. First, something must have been officially granted or issued in the first place — a right, a license, a document, a permission, or an offer. Second, the person or authority who has the power to cancel it must make a deliberate, active decision to do so. Revocation never happens on its own; someone must consciously pull the trigger. Third, the cancellation must be communicated — it takes effect once it is formally declared or received by the relevant party.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

Revocation appears across many important real-life contexts, and knowing these will help you recognize and use the word naturally.

In the world of driving, license revocation is one of the most common uses. If someone commits serious traffic violations — such as driving while intoxicated — the government can permanently cancel their driving license. This is called revocation, and it is more severe than a suspension, which only pauses the license temporarily.

In law and contracts, an offer made by one party can be revoked before the other party accepts it. Once revoked, the offer completely ceases to exist, and the other party can no longer accept it.

In the context of wills and inheritance, a person can revoke their will at any time while they are still alive. They do this by writing a new will or deliberately destroying the old one. The old document loses all its legal power the moment it is revoked.

In professional settings, licensed professionals such as doctors, lawyers, nurses, and architects can have their licenses to practice revoked by the relevant regulatory body if they violate professional standards or commit misconduct. They can no longer legally work in their profession until — and unless — the license is reinstated.

In digital and cybersecurity contexts, revocation refers to the cancellation of access rights, security certificates, or tokens. For example, if an employee leaves a company, their access to company systems may be revoked immediately, cutting off all permissions.

A power of attorney — a legal document giving one person the authority to act on another person's behalf — can also be revoked by the person who granted it, at any time, as long as they have the mental capacity to do so.
How Revocation Differs from Similar Words

This is one of the trickier parts of the word, so pay close attention.

Revocation is often confused with suspension. The key difference is permanence. A suspension is temporary — the thing is paused and can be restored after a set period. A revocation is a full, permanent cancellation. If your driver's license is suspended, you may get it back in three months. If it is revoked, it is gone entirely, and getting it back requires a formal re-application process, if it is even possible at all.

Revocation and cancellation are close in meaning, but revocation is far more formal and specific. Revocation always implies that something officially granted by an authority is being officially withdrawn by that same authority. Cancellation is a broader, more everyday word — you can cancel a dinner reservation or a Netflix subscription, but you would not use "revocation" in those situations.

Revocation and nullification are related but different. Nullification means declaring that something was never valid to begin with — it retroactively wipes out the past. Revocation, on the other hand, acknowledges that something was perfectly valid when it was issued, but is being ended now, going forward. Revocation does not erase the past; it closes the door on the future.

Revocation and termination differ in that termination usually describes something ending naturally — such as a contract reaching its agreed expiry date. Revocation is always a deliberate, often early, cancellation made by a decision of the granting authority, not a natural conclusion.

Revocation is always an active, deliberate act — it requires someone with the proper authority to make it happen. It is never accidental or automatic.

Revocation is serious and formal. You would not say someone "revoked" your invitation to a birthday party — you would say they canceled it. Revocation belongs to the language of law, institutions, official documents, and formal authority.

Revocation typically takes effect immediately or from the moment it is officially communicated, unless the revocation document specifically states a different date.

Once something is revoked, the original grant no longer exists. Getting it back usually requires starting the whole process fresh — applying again, being re-approved, and receiving a new grant.

Understanding the different forms of this word will help you use it correctly in any situation.

The verb form is "revoke" — it describes the action itself. For example: "The court decided to revoke his license." The past tense and past participle is "revoked," used as in: "Her license was revoked last year." The adjective form "revocable" describes something that is capable of being revoked — for example, "a revocable trust" is one that can be canceled by its creator. The opposite, and arguably more important, adjective is "irrevocable," which describes something that absolutely cannot be revoked or undone — for example, an irrevocable decision or an irrevocable letter of credit. This word appears very frequently in legal and financial documents, and it signals the highest level of finality and permanence. Finally, "revocation" itself — your noun — refers to the act or the instance of revoking something, as in: "The revocation of her medical license ended her career."
One-Line Summary to Anchor It All

Revocation is the formal, official cancellation of something previously granted — a right, a license, a will, an offer, or a permission — by the authority that originally issued it, ending its validity going forward, permanently.
13835:
To revoke something means to officially cancel or take it back — especially something that was given, granted, or decided in the past, and that had been giving someone a right, a power, or a permission.

The essential idea is this: something existed, it was valid, it allowed someone to do something or have something — and now it is being officially ended by the person or authority who originally granted it.

Think of it this way: when you revoke something, you are essentially saying, "What I gave you before? I am taking it back. It no longer counts."

This is important. You can cancel almost anything — a dinner reservation, a Netflix subscription, a plan with a friend. These are simple, everyday cancellations.

Revoke is different. It is a stronger, more formal, and more specific action. It almost always involves:

1. Something officially granted in the past — a license, a right, a permission, a legal document, an offer, or a privilege that came from an authority or a person in a position of power.

2. An official act of withdrawal — revocation is rarely casual. It is a deliberate, authoritative decision to declare that thing null and void, meaning it no longer has any legal or official standing.

3. A clear before and after — before the revocation, the thing was valid. After the revocation, it is not.
Who Can Revoke, and What Can Be Revoked?

A. Authorities and institutions revoke things like:

  • A driver's license — A court or government body can revoke someone's license if they drive dangerously or break the law. Once revoked, that person is no longer legally allowed to drive.
  • A professional license — A medical board can revoke a doctor's license for serious misconduct. That doctor can no longer legally practice medicine.
  • A passport — A government can revoke a citizen's passport, meaning that person can no longer use it for travel.
  • A permit — A business permit can be revoked if the business breaks regulations.
  • A law or decree — A government can revoke a law or an order it previously put in place, cancelling its effect entirely.

B. Organizations or employers revoke things like:

  • A job offer — A company can revoke a job offer if they discover the candidate was dishonest, or if circumstances change before the person starts.
  • Membership or access — A club or institution can revoke someone's membership for violating rules.

C. Individuals can also revoke things like:

  • An invitation — If someone behaves badly, you can revoke their invitation to your event.
  • An offer — If you offered to sell something to someone and they haven't accepted yet, you can revoke the offer.
  • A will — A person can revoke a will they wrote, making it invalid, and write a new one.
  • Consent — Someone who has given permission for something can revoke that consent, withdrawing their agreement.

Notice something common in all of the above: the thing being revoked was always real and valid before. You cannot revoke something that never existed or was never granted in the first place. This is central to the word's meaning. There must always be a prior granting — and then a withdrawal of that granting.

Once something is revoked, it is no longer in force. The person who held the right or privilege loses it. It is generally a permanent action — revocation is not the same as a temporary suspension (where something is paused and can be restored). When something is revoked, it is gone, and getting it back would typically require a fresh application or appeal, not just waiting.

Revoke is a formal word. You will mostly encounter it in legal, official, governmental, medical, and institutional settings. In everyday speech, people might simply say "take back" or "cancel," but when writing or speaking formally — in documents, news reports, legal proceedings, or professional contexts — "revoke" is the precise and appropriate word.
Synonyms — and How They Differ Slightly

Understanding how nearby words differ sharpens your understanding of "revoke."

  • Repeal — Used specifically for laws and legislation. A parliament repeals a law. You wouldn't say a driver's license was repealed.
  • Annul — Means to declare that something never legally existed at all. Most famously used for marriages. It's stronger than revoke.
  • Withdraw — To pull something back, often before it takes full effect (e.g., withdraw an application, withdraw troops). Less formal and more general than revoke.
  • Cancel — Broad and casual. Used for everyday things like events, orders, and plans. Does not carry the official weight of revoke.
  • Rescind — Nearly identical to revoke, and often interchangeable in formal/legal use. Rescind is used for contracts, orders, and decisions.

Revoke sits in the middle of this group — official and authoritative, focused specifically on cancelling something that granted a right or privilege.

• The judge revoked the defendant's bail after he violated the conditions of his release.
  • Her teaching certificate was revoked following the investigation.
  • The government revoked the executive order that had been in place for three years.
  • I revoke my permission — you no longer have my consent to use that photograph.
  • The company revoked the job offer when the background check revealed false information on his résumé.
  • He revoked his original will and wrote a new one before his death.
To revoke = to officially and formally cancel or take back something that was previously granted — a right, a license, a permission, an offer, or a privilege — so that it is no longer valid.
13836:
A revolt is when a group of people says "enough" — and then does something about it. It is a collective act of resistance against someone or something that holds power over them, whether that's a government, a ruler, an institution, or a set of rules they are forced to live under. The people in a revolt are not just unhappy. They have reached a breaking point, and they are actively pushing back.

Think of it this way: imagine a king who overtaxes his people, starves them, and punishes them for speaking up. For years, the people suffer quietly. Then one day, they rise up together — they refuse to obey, they take to the streets, they fight back. That collective act of rising up is a revolt.
The Full Range of Its Meaning

A revolt does not always mean swords and bloodshed, though it certainly can. It exists on a wide spectrum.

On one end, you have a violent, armed uprising — soldiers turning against their own army commanders, citizens taking up weapons against a government, enslaved people fighting for their freedom. These are loud, dramatic, and dangerous revolts.

On the other end, a revolt can be quieter but still powerful — workers refusing to work until their demands are met, students refusing to follow unjust school rules as a group, citizens loudly and collectively rejecting a new law. The defining feature is not violence, but defiance. A revolt always involves people rejecting authority they are supposed to submit to.

This is important: a revolt almost always flows upward. The weaker group revolts against the stronger one. The governed revolt against those who govern. The employees revolt against the management. The ordinary people revolt against the powerful elite.

You would not typically say that a king staged a revolt against his own peasants — because the king already has the power. The word "revolt" carries within it the idea of people fighting back from a position of less power, refusing to accept control they find unjust, unbearable, or wrong.

A revolt can be a massive historical event, like a nationwide uprising that shakes an entire country. But the word also works in smaller, more everyday situations.

A single classroom of students collectively refusing to take an unfair exam could be called a minor revolt. Workers at one factory walking off the job together in protest is a revolt. Even within a family, if all the children band together and refuse to follow an unreasonable rule set by their parents, someone might jokingly call it a revolt.

So while the word often appears in serious historical contexts, it is flexible enough to describe any scaled-down act of group defiance.
How It Feels: The Emotional Core

When you read the word "revolt," you should sense something urgent and passionate underneath it. A revolt is not a polite disagreement. It is not a formal complaint filed through proper channels. It carries heat — frustration that has built up over time and finally spilled over. There is a sense of moral energy to it: the people in a revolt usually believe, deeply and sincerely, that what they are fighting against is wrong and must be stopped.

This is why the word "revolt" carries a degree of sympathy toward those doing the revolting, at least in most modern usage. When you hear "a peasant revolt," your instinct is often to understand why the peasants reached that point — not to side automatically with the rulers they opposed.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Since "revolt," "rebellion," "revolution," "riot," and "protest" are often used near each other, it helps to know how "revolt" sits among them.

A protest is the mildest — people expressing disagreement openly, but still largely within accepted rules of society. A revolt is stronger and more defiant; it involves actively refusing authority or fighting against it.

A rebellion is very close to a revolt in meaning and the two are often interchangeable. If there is any subtle difference, a rebellion tends to suggest a more sustained, organized effort, while a revolt can be more spontaneous — a sudden eruption of resistance.

A revolution is bigger in scale and consequence. A revolution typically succeeds in fundamentally overturning the existing power structure and replacing it with something new. A revolt may or may not succeed, and even if it does, it doesn't necessarily rebuild an entire system from the ground up. You could say that many revolts fail, but a successful revolt that completely transforms society might eventually be called a revolution.

A riot is largely about disorder, chaos, and violence — it doesn't necessarily have a clear political goal or unified leadership. A revolt, even when it turns violent, implies more intention and purpose behind it.

There is a second, less common way "revolt" is used as a noun — to describe a strong inner feeling of disgust or repulsion. When something is deeply offensive to your senses or your values, you might experience an inner revolt. For example: "He looked at the corrupt agreement in front of him, and felt a revolt rise within him." Here, the revolt is not a public uprising — it is an internal one. Something inside the person is rejecting what they are seeing.

This usage is less frequent, and in everyday language, words like "revulsion" or "disgust" are more commonly used for this feeling. But it's worth knowing because you will encounter it in literature and formal writing.

A revolt (noun) is a forceful, collective act of resistance — people standing up against authority, power, or control they refuse to accept any longer. It lives between a protest (which is milder) and a revolution (which is larger and more transformative). It is driven by defiance, moral urgency, and the refusal to submit. It can be violent or non-violent, massive or small-scale, historical or everyday. And in a more personal sense, it can also describe the deep inner feeling of repulsion when something goes against everything you believe or value.
13837: "Revolt" is a powerful word. It carries strong emotions — whether anger, resistance, or deep disgust. As a verb, it has two distinct meanings, and understanding both is key.
Meaning 1 — To Rise Up and Refuse to Obey

When people revolt, they rise up against someone or something that has power over them — a ruler, a government, a system — because they can no longer accept it. They refuse to obey, and they push back, often with force or organized action.

This sense of revolt is always about a group (or an individual) saying: "We will not accept this any longer." It is a dramatic, often dangerous act of defiance. It goes beyond simple disagreement or complaint — it is active, determined resistance.

Examples:

  • "The workers revolted against their cruel employer and refused to work."
  • "Citizens revolted against the government after years of oppression."
  • "The students revolted against the school's unfair rules."

Notice that this meaning is almost always followed by "against" — you revolt against something. You are pushing back at a force that has authority over you.

Degree and scale matter here. Revolting in this sense isn't just being quietly unhappy. It is a bold, open act of defiance. A person who disagrees silently hasn't revolted. The revolt happens when the defiance becomes visible, active, and collective.
Meaning 2 — To Fill Someone With Disgust or Horror

The second meaning of "revolt" is completely different in feel. Here, something revolts you — meaning it fills you with a strong sense of disgust, repulsion, or horror. Your stomach turns. You feel like looking away, stepping back, or recoiling.

In this meaning, "revolt" works like a trigger: something external causes an intense, unpleasant reaction inside you.

Examples:

  • "The sight of the rotting food revolted her."
  • "His cruel behavior revolted everyone in the room."
  • "The violence in the video revolted me — I had to turn it off."

Notice a structural difference here: in this meaning, the thing that is disgusting does the revolting. The food revolts her. The behavior revolts everyone. Something acts on you and causes revulsion.

This is also where the adjective "revolting" comes from — if something is revolting, it means it is deeply disgusting or offensive. You'll hear people say, "That smell is absolutely revolting," meaning it causes a strong, unpleasant physical or emotional reaction.

How strong is this feeling? Strong. "Revolt" in this sense isn't mild dislike. It isn't "I don't love this." It is a gut-level reaction — the kind of disgust that makes your body respond, not just your mind. Think of the feeling you get when you see something truly horrifying or deeply wrong. That is the level of intensity this word carries.

At first, the two meanings seem very different — one is about rebellion, the other about disgust. But there is a thread that connects them: a deep, powerful rejection.

When people revolt against a ruler, they are rejecting authority so completely that they are willing to fight it. When something revolts you, your entire being rejects it — physically and emotionally. In both cases, the word signals that something has crossed a line, and the response is not quiet or polite. It is visceral and strong.

Who does the revolting changes the meaning. This is the most important thing to watch for when you read or hear this word:

  • If people are revolting (or revolting against something), you are looking at Meaning 1 — rebellion.
  • If something is revolting someone (a smell, a sight, a behavior), you are looking at Meaning 2 — disgust.

Context almost always makes it clear. "The crowd revolted against the king" is rebellion. "The smell revolted the crowd" is disgust. Pay attention to what comes before and after the word.

"Revolting" as an adjective always means disgusting, never rebellious. So "a revolting meal" means a deeply disgusting meal — not a meal that is staging an uprising.

"Revolt" as a verb lives in the territory of extreme reactions. Whether it describes people fighting back against oppression or a person's gut-wrenching response to something horrible, it is never a mild word. It always signals that something has gone beyond what can be quietly tolerated — and that the response is powerful, emotional, and undeniable.
13838:
Revolting describes something that causes a strong, powerful feeling of disgust — the kind that makes you want to immediately back away, look away, or even feel physically sick.

It is not a mild word. When you say something is revolting, you mean it triggers a very intense, gut-level rejection — a sharp, stomach-turning reaction from either your body, your mind, or both.

To truly understand "revolting," you first need to understand what disgust feels like. Disgust is not just dislike. It is a deep, intense negative reaction — the kind that makes your face scrunch up, your stomach churn, or your appetite disappear in an instant.

"Revolting" describes the thing causing that feeling.

So when you say something is revolting, you are saying: this thing is so offensive or unpleasant that it triggers that powerful disgust reaction in me.

"Revolting" is a strong word — it sits near the top of the disgust scale. Think of it this way:

Unpleasant → Distasteful → Disgusting → Revolting → Nauseating

If you say something is merely unpleasant, you are mildly bothered. If you say it is revolting, you are saying it is extreme — deeply, seriously offensive to your senses or your values. It is not an exaggeration; it is an expression of genuine, strong revulsion.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Revolting?

1. Things that offend your physical senses

Anything that looks, smells, or tastes deeply unpleasant:

  • A revolting odor from rotting meat.
  • The revolting sight of a pile of insects.
  • Food left out for days can become revolting.

2. Behavior or actions that violate decency

When someone does something morally ugly or socially shocking:

  • A revolting act of cruelty toward an animal.
  • His revolting rudeness shocked everyone at the table.

3. Ideas, attitudes, or content

Things that offend your values or sense of right and wrong:

  • Some people find certain political ideas revolting.
  • Revolting content that no one should have to see.

4. A person (used harshly)

You can call a person revolting, but this is a very strong judgment — it means their behavior, attitude, or manner is deeply offensive to you:

  • He was a revolting individual — selfish, cruel, and utterly indecent.

1. The smell from the blocked drain was absolutely revolting — I had to leave the room immediately.
  2. She found his comments about other people revolting and walked away from the conversation.
  3. The food in the back of the refrigerator had gone bad and looked completely revolting.
  4. The conditions in which the workers were kept were revolting — no human being should live that way.
  5. He said something so revolting at dinner that the entire table fell silent.
  6. I try to be open-minded, but some forms of cruelty are simply revolting — there is no other word for it.
  7. The scene in the horror film was visually revolting, so I had to look away.

Understanding the words around "revolting" helps sharpen your understanding of the word itself.

  • Disgusting — the closest and most common synonym. "Revolting" is basically a slightly more vivid, intense version of "disgusting."
  • Repulsive — implies something strongly pushes you away; you feel an urge to retreat or stay far from it.
  • Nauseating — specifically suggests it makes you feel physically sick, almost to the point of vomiting.
  • Repugnant — a formal word, most often used for moral disgust; something deeply at odds with your values or principles.
  • Vile — means extremely wicked, dirty, or morally rotten. Often used for behavior or character.
  • Abhorrent — a formal, very strong word expressing complete moral rejection.
  • Loathsome — means it inspires both hatred and disgust together.
  • Offensive — milder; something that upsets or disrespects you, but not necessarily to the extreme degree "revolting" implies.
  • Distasteful — the mildest of the group; something unpleasant and not to your liking, but far from extreme.

Among all these, "revolting" sits closest to "disgusting" and "repulsive," but with an emphasis on a strong, immediate, visceral reaction.

Words that mean the opposite — things that attract you, please you, or appeal to your senses:

  • Appealing, attractive, pleasant, delightful, charming, inviting, agreeable, lovely.
How It Is Used in Sentences

"Revolting" almost always comes directly before a noun, or after a linking verb like is, was, seems, or looks:

  • Before a noun: a revolting smell / a revolting idea / revolting behavior
  • After a verb: The food was revolting. / It looked revolting. / The idea seems revolting.

It is very commonly strengthened with words like absolutely, utterly, completely, or truly to emphasize just how strong the reaction is:

  • Absolutely revolting.
  • Utterly revolting.
  • Completely revolting.
Revolting means: so deeply unpleasant, offensive, or disgusting — whether to your senses or to your moral values — that it triggers a powerful, immediate feeling of disgust and rejection.

Think of it this way: the word "revolting" is related to the feeling of revulsion — that sudden, involuntary feeling of being pushed away and sickened by something. When something causes revulsion, it is revolting. The two words are built from the same root idea: a strong, almost physical turning away from something.
13839:
"Revolution" means a complete and total turning. Think of a wheel making one full spin — it goes all the way around and arrives at a new position. That feeling of something going all the way around, fully and completely, is the soul of this word. Depending on the context, this "complete turning" can refer to a physical motion, a political event, or a sweeping change in society or ideas.

The word has three main families of meaning, and understanding each one will make you fully fluent with this word.
Meaning 1: A Single Complete Circle or Orbit (Physical/Scientific)

In science and mechanics, a revolution is one complete trip around a central point. This is the most literal, concrete sense of the word.

Examples:

  • The Earth makes one revolution around the Sun every year. That is what a "year" actually is — one full orbit, one revolution.
  • A car engine's performance is measured in RPM, which stands for revolutions per minute — how many complete spins the engine makes in a minute.
  • A spinning top makes many revolutions per second before it slows down and falls.

Key point: In this sense, the word is about rotation — something moving in a circle and completing that circle fully. One revolution = one full loop. It is precise and measurable.
Meaning 2: The Violent Overthrow of a Government or Social System (Political)

This is the meaning most people think of when they hear "revolution," and it is arguably the most powerful one. A political revolution is when the people of a country forcibly overturn the existing power structure — not just replacing one leader with another, but tearing down the entire old system and replacing it with something fundamentally new.

Examples:

  • The French Revolution (1789) — The ordinary people of France rose up against the king and the aristocracy. The monarchy was abolished. The entire social order was dismantled and rebuilt.
  • The American Revolution (1776) — The American colonies rejected British rule entirely and created an independent nation with a completely new system of government.
  • The Russian Revolution (1917) — The Tsar (emperor) was overthrown, and the country was rebuilt as a communist state.

What makes it a revolution and not just a change of leadership?

This is important. A revolution is not simply swapping one leader for another. A revolution is when:

  1. The whole system changes, not just who is in charge.
  2. It happens rapidly — often through force, uprising, or dramatic confrontation.
  3. The old order is destroyed — not reformed, not tweaked, but fundamentally ended.
  4. A new order is built in its place — new laws, new values, new power structures.

Think of it this way: If you repaint a house, that is reform. If you knock the house down and build a completely different kind of structure from the ground up, that is revolution.
Meaning 3: A Complete and Transformative Change in Any Field (Figurative)

The word "revolution" is also used more broadly to describe any dramatic, sweeping, and irreversible change — even outside of politics. When something changes so completely that the world before it and the world after it look almost unrecognizable from each other, people call it a revolution.

Examples:

  • The Industrial Revolution — When machines replaced hand labour in the 18th and 19th centuries, it did not just change how goods were made. It changed where people lived, how they worked, family structures, the economy, and the entire rhythm of human life. Nothing was the same after it.
  • The Digital Revolution — The rise of computers and the internet transformed communication, business, entertainment, relationships, and access to information so completely that we now speak of a "before" and "after."
  • "The discovery of penicillin was a revolution in medicine." — Doctors could now cure infections that had previously killed millions. The entire landscape of medicine shifted.
  • "Her book caused a revolution in how scientists think about memory."

Key point: When used this way, "revolution" is not just saying that something changed. It is saying that the change was so deep, total, and fast that it rewrote the rules entirely. It implies: nothing will ever be the same again.

Understanding what a word is not is just as important as understanding what it is.

Revolution vs. Reform
Reform is change within the existing system — gradual, controlled, and working with the current structure. Revolution is change of the system — it breaks the existing structure rather than improving it. A government that passes new laws to reduce poverty is reforming. A government that is overthrown and replaced with a new one is revolutionary.

Revolution vs. Evolution
Evolution (in the everyday sense) means slow, gradual change over a long period of time. Revolution is the opposite — it is fast, dramatic, and often sudden. Evolution is a river slowly carving a canyon over thousands of years. Revolution is an earthquake.

Revolution vs. Rebellion / Revolt
A rebellion or revolt is an attempt to overthrow a system. A revolution implies that the attempt succeeded and that a new order was actually established. Every revolution begins as a rebellion, but not every rebellion becomes a revolution.

Revolution vs. Coup
A coup (short for coup d'état) is when a small group — usually the military — seizes power quickly. It changes who is in charge, but often leaves the deeper system intact. A revolution involves the masses (ordinary people), destroys the old system, and builds something genuinely new.
Degrees of the Word: Strong by Nature

"Revolution" is an inherently strong, serious word. It carries weight. When you use it, you are signalling that something is not minor or incremental. You are saying: this is total, this is fundamental, this is a before-and-after moment. Because of this, the word is sometimes used hyperbolically (exaggeratedly) in everyday speech or advertising — "This blender is a revolution in cooking!" — but careful writers and speakers use it only when something truly justifies that level of magnitude.

ContextWhat "revolution" means
  • In science/mechanics: One complete circular orbit or spin around a central point.
  • In politics/history: The violent, total overthrow of a government or social system, replacing it with something fundamentally new.
  • In general use: Any change so complete, fast, and far-reaching that it permanently transforms a field, society, or way of thinking.

The common thread across all three meanings is the idea of something going all the way around — completing a full turn, arriving at a place entirely different from where it started, with no going back.
